accuracy.evidence: Every fact checked: rainbow order red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (Newton's seven); planets Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune with Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet by the IAU in 2006; 30-day months are April, June, September, November, February 28/29, the other seven have 31 (m5 answer 12-4-1=7 is fixed by the rhyme, numeric params all give whole positive answers); because spelled b-e-c-a-u-s-e from Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants. Research claims match Dunlosky et al. 2013 (keyword mnemonic rated low utility, limited to recall) and Bellezza 1981.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the four slips teachers see with mnemonics: believing the trick holds the answer (step 2 prediction 'the sentence tells you', p4, m4, challenge 'cue' item), confusing two items with the same first letter (Mercury and Mars decoys with a specific message), right letter but wrong place (compass step rejects a word in the wrong slot, spelling step names a-u order) and using a trick where understanding is needed (m6). Adult text names each mistake and the self-test fix.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmnem is the only lab where the child decodes and builds first-letter cues: letter-to-word decoding for the rainbow and planets, building a compass sentence from letter tiles, picking months from a rhyme and spelling a word from its sentence. flagmem (how memory works) models short and long-term stores and flagrecall (retrieval practice) runs a self-quiz; neither uses mnemonic cues. The 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child has to turn each word into its item: tapping the colour for the boxed word, the planet for each word with Moon and Sun decoys refused, choosing any word with the right first letter for N, E, S, W (shows the trick is theirs to make), finding the four 30-day months in a calendar grid from the rhyme, and tapping letters to spell because. Each wrong tap is rejected with a reason, so progress needs the idea, not guessing.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'My and Method both start with M. How do you know which is Mercury?' (the sentence tells you / either is fine), 'Which of these has 30 days?' (July or August, the common slip) and 'In because, which letter comes after c?' (u, the usual misspelling becuase). Each is revealed by the step that follows, with feedback naming the prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge has 12 distinct feedback messages for wrong picks: Gave read as grey or gold, 30-day months confused with 31-day ones, Mars put before Mercury, the trick thought to hold the answer, the 'a longer sentence' fix, and the spelling order a-u. Each message says why the pick is wrong in one short line, then the item repeats until right.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences with the hard words introduced once (mnemonic, memory trick) and passes the learner FK target in validate_lessons; adult text was rewritten to FK below 9.5 with sentences of 10-20 words. Lab instructions are under 20 words each and every item prompt is one sentence.

no_filler.evidence: No praise padding or 'in this lesson we will'; the content gate's filler regex passed. Each paragraph carries one idea: what a mnemonic is, the kinds, the limit, then for adults the curriculum link, why it works, mistakes and what the lab does.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 (390px) in light and dark for all six steps: the sentence chips wrap to two rows, answer tiles are a 3-column grid with tap targets well over 44px, and nothing overflows. The browser gate walk (Show me on desktop and iPhone 13) passed with no console errors.

accessibility.evidence: axe ran in both themes with no violations in the browser gate; every tile is a real button with an aria-label, the controls region has aria-label 'Lab controls', colour is never the only cue (each rainbow colour tile has its name, the boxed word is outlined as well as coloured), and the feedback line is announced in a live region by the kit.
